explanation.text:
(Pro. 25:1-28)

The character of these proverbs sustains the title (see Introduction).

also--refers to the former part of the book.

copied out--literally, "transferred," that is, from some other book to this; not given from memory.

bsb.text: These are additional proverbs of Solomon, which were copied by the men of Hezekiah king of Judah:

explanation.text: God's unsearchableness impresses us with awe (compare Isa 45:15; Rom 11:33). But kings, being finite, should confer with wise counsellors;

bsb.text: It is the glory of God to conceal a matter and the glory of kings to search it out.

explanation.text: Ye wisely keeping state secrets, which to common men are as inaccessible heights and depths.

bsb.text: As the heavens are high and the earth is deep, so the hearts of kings cannot be searched.

explanation.text: As separating impurities from ore leaves pure silver, so taking from a king wicked counsellors leaves a wise and beneficent government.

bsb.text: Remove the dross from the silver, and a vessel for a silversmith will come forth.

explanation.text: before--or, "in presence of," as courtiers stood about a king.

bsb.text: Remove the wicked from the king’s presence, and his throne will be established in righteousness.

explanation.text: Do not intrude into the presence of the king, for the elevation of the humble is honorable, but the humbling of the proud disgraceful (Luk 14:8-10).

bsb.text: Do not exalt yourself in the presence of the king, and do not stand in the place of great men;

explanation.text:
For better it is that it be said unto thee, Come up hither,.... It is much more to thine honour and credit to seat thyself in a place rather beneath than above thee; which being observed by some of the officers at court, or by him whose business it is to look after such things, he will beckon or call to thee to come up to a higher and more honourable place:

than that thou shouldest be put lower, in the presence of the prince whom thine eyes have seen; than that thou shouldest be thrust away with a severe rebuke for thy boldness and arrogance, in approaching too near the king's person, and taking the place of some great man, which did not become thee, and be forced down to a lower place, to thy great mortification; and the more, as this will be in the presence of the prince thou hadst the curiosity of seeing, and the ambition of making thyself acceptable to, by a gay and splendid appearance; and now with great disgrace turned out of his presence, or at least driven to a great distance from him. Our Lord seems to refer to this passage, in Luke 14:8.

bsb.text: for it is better to be told, “Come up here!” than to be demoted in the presence of the prince. Even what you have seen with your own eyes,

explanation.text:
(Compare Pro 3:30).

lest . . . shame--lest you do what you ought not, when shamed by defeat, or "lest thou art shut out from doing any thing."

bsb.text: do not bring hastily to court. Otherwise, what will you do in the end when your neighbor puts you to shame?

explanation.text:
(Compare Mat 5:25, Margin).

secret--that is, of your opponent, for his disadvantage, and so you be disgraced, not having discussed your difficulties with him.

bsb.text: Argue your case with your neighbor without betraying another’s confidence,

explanation.text:
Lest he that heareth it put thee to shame,.... Or, "reproach thee" with treachery and deceit. Either the person of whom it is told, or the person to whom it is told; who may make thee ashamed, either by fixing the odious character of a defamer, a whisperer, and backbiter, on thee; or by making a retaliation, and in his turn make known some secret things concerning thyself, which before were not known, and, now published, will be to thy disgrace;

and thine infamy turn not away; it shall stick so close to thee, that thou shalt never get clear of it as long as thou livest, or ever retrieve thy credit; the brand of infamy shall ever be upon thee.

bsb.text: lest he who hears you bring shame upon you, and your infamy never go away.

explanation.text:
a word fitly--literally, "quickly," as wheels roll, just in time. The comparison as apples . . . silver gives a like sense.

apples, etc.--either real apples of golden color, in a silver network basket, or imitations on silver embroidery.

bsb.text: A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in settings of silver.

explanation.text: Those who desire to know and do rightly, most highly esteem good counsel (Pro 9:9; Pro 15:31). The listening ear is better than one hung with gold.

bsb.text: Like an earring of gold or an ornament of fine gold is a wise man’s rebuke to a listening ear.

explanation.text: Snow from mountains was used to cool drinks; so refreshing is a faithful messenger (Pro 13:17).

bsb.text: Like the cold of snow in the time of harvest is a trustworthy messenger to those who send him; he refreshes the soul of his masters.

explanation.text:
clouds--literally, "vapors" (Jer 10:13), clouds only in appearance.

a false gift--promised, but not given.

bsb.text: Like clouds and wind without rain is the man who boasts of gifts never given.

explanation.text:
Gentleness and kindness overcome the most powerful and obstinate.

long forbearing--or, "slowness to anger" (Pro 14:29; Pro 15:18).

bsb.text: Through patience a ruler can be persuaded, and a gentle tongue can break a bone.

explanation.text: A comparison, as a surfeit of honey produces physical disgust, so your company, however agreeable in moderation, may, if excessive, lead your friend to hate you.

bsb.text: If you find honey, eat just what you need, lest you have too much and vomit it up.

explanation.text:
Withdraw thy foot from thy neighbour's house,.... Not but that it is commendable to be neighbourly and friendly, or for one neighbour to visit another; but then it should not be very frequent; a man should not be always or often at his neighbour's house. So the words may be rendered, "make thy foot precious" or "rare at thy neighbour's house"; be seldom there;

lest he be weary of thee, and so hate thee; or, "lest he be sated with thee"; filled with thy company to a loathing of it, as the stomach with eating too much honey, and so his friendship be turned into hatred.

bsb.text: Seldom set foot in your neighbor’s house, lest he grow weary and hate you.

explanation.text:
A false witness is as destructive to reputation, as such weapons to the body (Pro 24:28).

beareth . . . witness--literally, "answereth questions," as before a judge, against his neighbor.

bsb.text: Like a club or sword or sharp arrow is a man who bears false witness against his neighbor.

explanation.text: Treachery annoys as well as deceives.

bsb.text: Like a broken tooth or a foot out of joint is confidence in a faithless man in time of trouble.

explanation.text: Not only is the incongruity of songs (that is, joyful) and sadness meant, but an accession of sadness, by want of sympathy, is implied.

bsb.text: Like one who removes a garment on a cold day or vinegar poured on a wound is one who sings songs to a heavy heart.

explanation.text: (Compare Mat 5:44; Rom 12:20). As metals are melted by heaping coals upon them, so is the heart softened by kindness.

bsb.text: If your enemy is hungry, give him food to eat, and if he is thirsty, give him water to drink.

explanation.text:
For thou shall heap coals of fire upon his head,.... Not to increase his punishment and damnation, the more aggravated by kindness shown him; but to bring him by such means to a sense of former injuries, and to shame for them, repentance of them, and love of the person injured, and carefulness for the future of doing him any further wrong;

and the Lord shall reward thee: with good things, for all the good done to thine enemy, whether it has the desired effect on him or not; or whether he rewards thee or not; see Romans 12:20.

bsb.text: For in so doing, you will heap burning coals on his head, and the LORD will reward you.

explanation.text: Better, "As the north wind bringeth forth (Psa 90:2) or produces rain, so does a concealed or slandering tongue produce anger."

bsb.text: As the north wind brings forth rain, so a backbiting tongue brings angry looks.

explanation.text: (Compare Pro 21:9, Pro 21:19).

bsb.text: Better to live on a corner of the roof than to share a house with a quarrelsome wife.

explanation.text:
(Compare Pro 25:13).

good news--that is, of some loved interest or absent friend, the more grateful as coming from afar.

bsb.text: Like cold water to a weary soul is good news from a distant land.

explanation.text: From troubled fountains and corrupt springs no healthy water is to be had, so when the righteous are oppressed by the wicked, their power for good is lessened or destroyed.

bsb.text: Like a muddied spring or a polluted well is a righteous man who gives way to the wicked.

explanation.text:
Satiety surfeits (Pro 25:16); so men who are self-glorious find shame.

is not glory--"not" is supplied from the first clause, or "is grievous," in which sense a similar word is used (Pro 27:2).

bsb.text: It is not good to eat too much honey or to search out one’s own glory.

explanation.text:
Such are exposed to the incursions of evil thoughts and successful temptations.

bsb.text: Like a city whose walls are broken down is a man who does not control his temper.
